tree.className: text-style-16-body-reg text-[var(--color-text-secondary)]

$ for c in /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/; do
    id=$(basename "$c")
    waiting=$(cat "$c/waiting" 2>/dev/null)
    [ "$waiting" -gt 0 ] && echo "conn=$id waiting=$waiting"
  done
conn=368 waiting=10
conn=523 waiting=15

tree.className: text-style-16-body-reg text-[var(--color-text-secondary)]

tree: The number of pending waiters across connections matched the D-state thread count exactly. The kernel was holding live FUSE connections, with no userspace daemon on the other end answering them.

tree.className: text-style-16-body-reg text-[var(--color-text-secondary)]

tree: But this is not how FUSE is supposed to behave: when the userspace daemon dies, the kernel is meant to abort all pending requests so that blocked readers wake up with

tree.className: rounded-[var(--radius-small)] bg-[var(--color-bg-secondary)] px-1.5 py-0.5 font-mono text-[0.9em]

tree: . The function that does this is

tree.className: text-[var(--color-text-accent)] underline decoration-1 underline-offset-2
rounded-[var(--radius-small)] bg-[var(--color-bg-secondary)] px-1.5 py-0.5 font-mono text-[0.9em]

tree: , and it was clearly not called for these connections.

tree.className: text-style-18-head-med text-[var(--color-title-default)] tracking-tight

tree: Step 5: Verify by forcing the connection closed

tree.className: text-style-16-body-reg text-[var(--color-text-secondary)]

tree: The FUSE control filesystem exposes an

tree.className: rounded-[var(--radius-small)] bg-[var(--color-bg-secondary)] px-1.5 py-0.5 font-mono text-[0.9em]

tree: file per connection that forces the kernel to tear it down regardless of who still holds a file descriptor ("fd") onto it. On a cordoned, otherwise-idle test node, we aborted the stuck connections:

tree.className: overflow-x-auto rounded-[var(--radius-large)] border border-[var(--color-stroke-default)] bg-[var(--color-bg-secondary)] p-4
font-mono text-[length:var(--text-fs-2)] leading-[var(--text-fs-2--line-height)] text-[var(--color-text-default)]

tree:
$ for c in /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/; do
    w=$(cat "$c/waiting" 2>/dev/null)
    [ "$w" -gt 0 ] && echo 1 > "$c/abort"
  done

tree.className: text-style-16-body-reg text-[var(--color-text-secondary)]

tree.className: rounded-[var(--radius-small)] bg-[var(--color-bg-secondary)] px-1.5 py-0.5 font-mono text-[0.9em]

tree: , which kept them holding their CUDA contexts, which is why the VRAM never came back.
